stages.name: Independent states
stages.desc: Cities, leagues and peoples outside the great powers

stages.name: Athens and its allies
stages.desc: Athens and the members of its alliances and naval league

stages.name: Persian and Carian rule
stages.desc: Held by the Persian Empire or its Carian satraps

stages.name: Kingdom of Macedon
stages.desc: Ruled directly by the Macedonian kings

stages.name: Under Macedonian hegemony
stages.desc: Allied to or dominated by Macedon

stages.name: In revolt against Macedon
stages.desc: Risen in arms against Macedonian power

states.name: West Macedonia
timeline: The highland cantons of Upper Macedonia, Elimeia, Orestis and Lyncus, under their own princes
Philip II defeats the Illyrians and absorbs Upper Macedonia into his kingdom

states.name: Epirus
timeline: The Molossian kings and the other peoples of Epirus, independent
Philip marries Olympias, a Molossian princess, sealing an alliance
Philip places Olympias' brother Alexander on the Molossian throne as a client king

states.name: Centre Macedonia
timeline: Pella, the royal capital of Macedon; the Chalcidian cities to the east, Stagira among them, are still independent
Philip captures Amphipolis on the Strymon
Philip conquers the Chalcidice: Olynthus is razed and Stagira destroyed
Aristotle teaches the young Alexander at Mieza; Stagira is rebuilt

states.name: East Macedonia and Thrace
timeline: Greek coastal cities such as Abdera and Thasos, and Thracian peoples inland
Philip seizes Krenides and the gold mines of Mount Pangaion and refounds it as Philippi

states.name: Mount Athos
timeline: The small Greek towns of the Acte peninsula, part of the Chalcidian world
Annexed with the rest of the Chalcidice after Philip's war

states.name: Thessalia
timeline: Thessalian cities and rival lords, among them the tyrants of Pherae
After the battle of the Crocus Field, Philip is made head of the Thessalian League
Thessalian cavalry joins the Greek revolt of the Lamian War
Antipater's victory at Crannon ends the revolt

states.name: Central Greece
timeline: Boeotia, Phocis, Locris and Euboea; Thebes is rising
Thebes defeats Sparta at Leuctra and leads Greece for a decade
Philip wins at Chaeronea; a Macedonian garrison holds Thebes
Alexander destroys Thebes after its revolt
Phocians and Locrians join the revolt, but Boeotia and Chalcis on Euboea stay with Macedon; Aristotle takes refuge in Chalcis

states.name: Attica
timeline: Athens, a democracy, rebuilding a web of allies
Athens founds the Second Athenian League, a naval alliance of free states
Defeated at Chaeronea, Athens joins Philip's League of Corinth
On news of Alexander's death, Athens leads the Greek revolt of the Lamian War
Defeated, Athens must accept a Macedonian garrison and a narrower franchise

states.name: Peloponnese
timeline: Sparta and its Peloponnesian allies
The battle of Mantinea leaves no Greek city strong enough to lead
The Peloponnesian states except Sparta join Philip's League of Corinth
King Agis III of Sparta leads a revolt against Macedon
Agis is defeated and killed at Megalopolis

states.name: West Greece
timeline: Achaea, Elis and the Aetolian and Acarnanian peoples
After Chaeronea, the western Greeks come under Macedonian leadership
The Aetolians become Athens' chief allies in the Lamian War
The Aetolians fight on after the defeat at Crannon

states.name: Crete
timeline: Crete's many cities stay outside the mainland's leagues
Spartan agents, paid by Persia, win over Cretan cities

states.name: South Aegean
timeline: The Cyclades and Dodecanese, between Sparta, Athens and Persia
Rhodes and most of the Cyclades join the Second Athenian League
After the Social War, Rhodes and Kos fall under the Carian dynasty that rules for Persia; the Cyclades stay with Athens
Alexander's fleet takes the islands; a Macedonian garrison holds Rhodes
Rhodes expels its Macedonian garrison on news of Alexander's death

states.name: North Aegean
timeline: Chios allies with Athens; Mytilene on Lesbos is already Athens' ally
Chios breaks with Athens in the Social War; Lesbos, Lemnos and Samos stay Athenian
Aristotle and Theophrastus study the animals of the lagoon at Pyrrha on Lesbos
Memnon's Persian fleet takes Chios and Lesbos
Macedonian admirals win back the islands
Samos is given back to the Samians after decades of Athenian settlers

states.name: Ionian Islands
timeline: Corcyra and the western isles, independent
Corcyra and Cephallenia join Athens' naval league
With Athens' league dissolved after Chaeronea, the western isles stand apart

events.title: Aristotle is born
events.text: Aristotle is born at Stagira in the Chalcidice; his father Nicomachus is physician to King Amyntas III of Macedon.

events.title: Demosthenes is born
events.text: The orator who will lead Athens' resistance to Macedon is born in the same year as Aristotle.

events.title: Chios allies with Athens
events.text: Chios and Athens swear a defensive alliance, a first step toward a new Athenian league.

events.title: Second Athenian League
events.text: Athens founds a naval league of free allies against Sparta; islands across the Aegean join.

events.title: Corcyra joins Athens
events.text: The Athenian admiral Timotheus brings Corcyra into the league.

events.title: Battle of Leuctra
events.text: Thebes defeats Sparta, ending Spartan dominance on land.

events.title: To the Academy
events.text: At seventeen, Aristotle joins Plato's school outside Athens; he stays twenty years.

events.title: Battle of Mantinea
events.text: Thebes wins, but its general Epaminondas is killed; no Greek city is left strong enough to lead.

events.title: Philip II rules Macedon
events.text: Philip II takes power in Macedon and rebuilds its army.

events.title: Upper Macedonia united
events.text: Philip defeats the Illyrians and brings the highland cantons under the crown.

events.title: Amphipolis falls
events.text: Philip captures Amphipolis on the Strymon, a city Athens had long claimed.

events.title: The Social War
events.text: Chios, Rhodes, Kos and Byzantium revolt against Athens' league.

events.title: Philippi founded
events.text: Philip seizes Krenides and its gold mines and refounds it as Philippi.

events.title: Alexander is born
events.text: Philip's son Alexander is born at Pella.

events.title: Rhodes under Caria
events.text: Rhodes falls under the Carian dynasty of Mausolus, Persia's satrap.

events.title: Siege of Methone
events.text: Philip takes Athens' ally Methone and loses an eye to an arrow.

events.title: Crocus Field
events.text: Philip defeats the Phocians in Thessaly and becomes head of the Thessalian League.

events.title: Olynthus razed
events.text: Philip destroys Olynthus and enslaves its people; Stagira is destroyed in the same war.

events.title: Plato dies
events.text: Plato dies in Athens; his nephew Speusippus takes over the Academy, and Aristotle leaves.

events.title: Guest of Hermias
events.text: Aristotle joins Hermias, ruler of Atarneus and Assos, and marries his niece Pythias.

events.title: Mytilene
events.text: Aristotle moves to Lesbos and settles at Mytilene, its chief city.

events.title: The lagoon at Pyrrha
events.text: With Theophrastus of Eresos, Aristotle studies the animals of the lagoon at Pyrrha.

events.title: Tutor at Mieza
events.text: Philip invites Aristotle to teach Alexander, then thirteen, at the shrine of the Nymphs at Mieza.

events.title: Stagira rebuilt
events.text: Plutarch says Philip rebuilt Stagira and freed its people as Aristotle's fee.

events.title: Epirus as client
events.text: Philip places Olympias' brother Alexander on the throne of the Molossians.

events.title: Hermias betrayed
events.text: Persia's general Mentor seizes Hermias by a trick; he is taken to the king and executed.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.text: Philip and the young Alexander defeat Athens and Thebes; Macedon becomes master of Greece.

events.title: League of Corinth
events.text: The Greek states except Sparta swear peace and alliance under Philip's leadership.

events.title: Philip assassinated
events.text: Philip is murdered at Aegae; Alexander becomes king at twenty.

events.title: Thebes destroyed
events.text: After a revolt, Alexander razes Thebes and enslaves its people.

events.title: The Lyceum opens
events.text: Back in Athens, Aristotle begins teaching at the Lyceum gymnasium outside the city walls.

events.title: Honoured at Delphi
events.text: Delphi honours Aristotle and Callisthenes for listing the victors of the Pythian Games.

events.title: Alexander crosses over
events.text: Alexander's army crosses the Hellespont to invade the Persian Empire.

events.title: Persians take Lesbos
events.text: Memnon's Persian fleet besieges Mytilene and takes Chios and Lesbos.

events.title: Islands recovered
events.text: Macedonian admirals win back Chios, Lesbos and Kos from the Persians.

events.title: Agis' revolt
events.text: Agis III of Sparta rises against Macedon; Antipater crushes him at Megalopolis.

events.title: Athens rises
events.text: When news comes that Alexander has died in Babylon, Athens votes for war on Macedon.

events.title: Charged with impiety
events.text: The priest Eurymedon accuses Aristotle of impiety over his hymn to Hermias; Aristotle leaves for Chalcis.

events.title: Siege of Lamia
events.text: The Greek allies trap Antipater in Lamia, giving the Lamian War its name.

events.title: Rhodes expels garrison
events.text: Rhodes drives out its Macedonian garrison on news of Alexander's death.

events.title: Battle of Amorgos
events.text: Macedon's fleet defeats the Athenian navy, ending Athens' sea power.

events.title: Battle of Crannon
events.text: Antipater defeats the Greek allies in Thessaly; Athens must accept a garrison.

events.title: Death at Chalcis
events.text: Aristotle dies of an illness at Chalcis, in his early sixties; Theophrastus inherits the school.

events.title: Demosthenes dies
events.text: Hunted by Antipater's men, Demosthenes takes poison on the island of Kalaureia.

chartNote: Share of the area of modern Greece by the power that dominated each of today's regions. The ancient Greek world was hundreds of cities and peoples, and most regions held several at once; the map shows the dominant one, a deliberate simplification. Regions are today's boundaries, and dates are approximate (Athenian years ran from midsummer, so many events fall across two of our years).
